title: The Proptotic Orbit: Anchoring and the Asymmetric Eye
subtitle: Unilateral proptosis in treated Graves' disease
coverDescription: Sinonasal exclusion in unilateral proptosis, the sight-threat gate, the lid measurement that changes the EUGOGO category, tendon sparing on orbital CT, activity versus severity, treatment timing, audiologic responsibility for teprotumumab, and applying a study to a patient it did not enroll.

steps.title: Step 1/10: The Diagnosis She Arrives With
steps.scenario: A 43-year-old woman is referred to your otolaryngology clinic by endocrinology. Over the past six months her right eye has become progressively more prominent, and she describes a constant deep ache behind it. She has Graves' disease, diagnosed eight months ago, and has been taking methimazole 5 mg daily for six months. She has no other medical history.
steps.media: Load image: Frontal clinical photograph at conversational distance, downscaled. Asymmetry is visible; lid margins are not measurable. No caption, no laterality marker.
steps.question: She already carries a diagnosis that explains her eye. Which line of questioning is most likely to change your differential rather than confirm it?

options.text: (A) Adherence to methimazole and her current hyperthyroid symptoms
(B) Nasal obstruction, epistaxis, reduced sense of smell, and cheek or lip numbness
(C) Family history of thyroid disease and other autoimmune conditions
(D) Recent upper respiratory infection, periorbital redness, and fever

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

Why this is the trap: a documented thyroid diagnosis captures the differential before the examination begins. The finding that should unsettle you is not the proptosis but its asymmetry, and unilateral proptosis is an otolaryngology differential: sinonasal malignancy invading the orbit, IgG4-related orbital disease, orbital lymphoma, and carotid-cavernous fistula all present this way.

On the distractors: A and C confirm what you already know. D is the right kind of thinking applied to the wrong tempo, since an acute infective framing does not fit a six-month course.

Her answers: right eye prominent before the left from onset, slow steady progression, no sudden change. No nasal obstruction, epistaxis, or smell change. Cheek and lip sensation normal. Current smoker, 10 pack-years, has not stopped. No radioactive iodine. TRAb was 3.2 U/L four months ago.

steps.title: Step 2/10: The Gate Before Everything Else
steps.scenario: Your history is complete and the sinonasal differential is now much less likely. You are ready to examine her and start ordering.
steps.question: Before you order any imaging or make any management decision, which single assessment must be documented?

options.text: (A) Visual acuity, color vision, and pupillary response
(B) Hertel exophthalmometry with the base setting recorded
(C) Thyroid function tests and TSH receptor antibody
(D) Intraocular pressure in primary gaze and in upgaze

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

All four belong in this workup. Only one of them is a gate. Dysthyroid optic neuropathy can progress in an eye that looks unremarkable from the outside, and proptosis magnitude correlates poorly with optic nerve compromise. Color desaturation and a relative afferent pupillary defect are the earliest reliable signs.

Attending rule: a management plan made without documented vision is unsafe no matter how correct the classification turns out to be. In this case the safety score is binary and it caps the ending.

Her results: visual acuity 20/25 right and 20/20 left with pinhole. Ishihara 14 of 14 in each eye. No relative afferent pupillary defect. Cornea clear on fluorescein, lagophthalmos 1 mm on the right.

steps.title: Step 3/10: The Measurement Nobody Records
steps.scenario: You continue the examination. Hertel exophthalmometry reads 20 mm on the right and 16 mm on the left, base 100 mm. Ductions show elevation limited by one grade on the right. She reports double vision only on sustained upgaze, worse when she is tired, absent in primary gaze and in reading position. Intraocular pressure is 18 mmHg in primary gaze and 24 mmHg in upgaze on the right.
steps.media: Load image: Close frontal photograph in primary gaze with both upper lid margins and both corneal light reflexes clearly in frame. Caption: 'Primary gaze, undilated.'
steps.question: Your examination so far cannot complete the EUGOGO severity classification. Which measurement is missing?

options.text: (A) Margin reflex distance 1, quantifying upper lid retraction
(B) Corneal sensation, to assess trigeminal involvement
(C) Visual fields to confrontation in each eye
(D) Slit lamp assessment of the anterior chamber

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

EUGOGO severity rests on four parameters: degree of lid retraction, soft tissue involvement, exophthalmos relative to the normal range for race and sex, and diplopia grade. Lid retraction is the one most often left out of the chart, because it requires a deliberate measurement rather than an impression.

Her measurement: MRD1 is 6.5 mm on the right and 4.0 mm on the left, against a normal of roughly 4 to 4.5 mm. That is upper lid retraction of more than 2 mm.

Hold onto this number. It is the finding that changes her category at Step 7, and it takes ninety seconds to obtain.

steps.title: Step 4/10: Reading the Orbit Yourself
steps.scenario: You order a CT of the orbits with contrast. Scroll the axial and coronal stacks before answering. The inferior and medial recti are enlarged bilaterally, more on the right, with sparing of the tendinous insertions. There is orbital fat expansion, no apical crowding, no bony erosion, and the paranasal sinuses are clear.
steps.media: Load video: Scrollable axial and coronal orbital CT stack, soft tissue window, unannotated. No arrows, no measurements, no radiologist impression.
steps.question: Which diagnosis does the sparing of the tendinous insertions argue most strongly against?

options.text: (A) Thyroid eye disease
(B) Idiopathic orbital myositis
(C) Orbital lymphoma
(D) Sinonasal malignancy with orbital invasion

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

Involvement of the muscle tendon is characteristic of idiopathic orbital myositis. Thyroid eye disease classically enlarges the muscle belly and spares the insertion, which is why the pattern here supports the diagnosis rather than merely being compatible with it.

The rest of the study completes the exclusion you began at Step 1. Clear sinuses and intact bone make sinonasal malignancy very unlikely, and the absence of a discrete mass argues against lymphoma. This is why the CT was worth ordering even though you already suspected the answer: it converts an assumption into an exclusion.

ENT relevance: orbital CT is a study otolaryngologists read routinely for sinus disease. Reading it for orbital muscle morphology uses the same images and a different search pattern.

steps.title: Step 5/10: One Result That Matters More Than the Others
steps.scenario: Laboratory results return: TSH 0.11 microIU/mL, free T4 1.11 ng/dL, T3 103 ng/dL, TSH receptor antibody 5.31 U/L. Her TSH receptor antibody four months ago was 3.2 U/L.
steps.question: Which single result most changes how you will counsel and follow her?

options.text: (A) TSH of 0.11 microIU/mL with a normal free T4
(B) T3 of 103 ng/dL
(C) TSH receptor antibody of 5.31 U/L, risen from 3.2 U/L
(D) Free T4 of 1.11 ng/dL

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

The rising TSH receptor antibody titre does two things at once. It confirms the diagnosis, and it is one of the EUGOGO risk factors for a worse orbital course, alongside smoking, thyroid dysfunction, radioactive iodine, and hypercholesterolemia. In a patient who is still smoking, a rising titre is the argument for a defined interval reassessment rather than discharge back to endocrinology.

On the others: a TSH of 0.11 with a normal free T4 and T3 is biochemical subclinical hyperthyroidism on treatment. It is worth a conversation with her endocrinologist about dose, but it does not change your orbital counseling. The free T4 and T3 are normal and change nothing.

Design note: a panel where every value is displayed as equally meaningful teaches nothing. The skill being tested is deciding which number to act on.

steps.title: Step 6/10: Activity, Computed Rather Than Announced
steps.scenario: Work through the seven-item Clinical Activity Score using only the findings you have obtained. Of the seven items, only spontaneous retrobulbar pain is present. Her eyelids and conjunctiva are not injected, there is no eyelid or caruncular swelling, no chemosis, and no pain on attempted up or down gaze.
steps.media: Load image: Interactive seven-item Clinical Activity Score checklist. The learner ticks the items; the app computes the total.
steps.question: Her CAS is 1 of 7, which places her below the threshold for active disease. Yet her proptosis has been progressing for six months. How do you reconcile these two facts?

options.text: (A) The seven-item score is cross-sectional; the ten-item follow-up score captures interval change, but her progression is slower than its one-to-three-month window
(B) Documented progression over any interval makes the disease active regardless of the score
(C) A score resting on a single positive item is unreliable and should be repeated before it is used
(D) Spontaneous retrobulbar pain is itself sufficient to classify the disease as active

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The seven-item CAS measures inflammation at a moment. The ten-item follow-up score adds an increase in proptosis of 2 mm or more, reduced ductions, and lost acuity, assessed over a one-to-three-month interval. Her progression is real but slower than that window, so it does not formally score.

Clinical pearl worth carrying out of this case: inactive is a measurement, not a promise. A CAS of 1 in a current smoker with a rising antibody titre is a reason to set a review date, not a reason to discharge.

This is the question the original version of this case did not ask. Announcing 'CAS less than 3' and moving on removes the only interesting part.

steps.title: Step 7/10: Severity, and a Correction to the Chart
steps.scenario: You now have everything you need. MRD1 6.5 mm right against 4.0 mm left. Hertel 20 mm right against 16 mm left. Diplopia on sustained upgaze, absent in primary gaze. Cornea clear, no relative afferent pupillary defect, acuity near normal. CAS 1 of 7.
steps.question: Using the EUGOGO severity criteria and the findings you have actually documented, how do you classify her?

options.text: (A) Mild Graves' orbitopathy
(B) Moderate-to-severe Graves' orbitopathy
(C) Sight-threatening Graves' orbitopathy
(D) Severity cannot be assigned until orbital MRI is obtained

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

Moderate-to-severe disease is not sight-threatening but carries enough impact to justify the risks of treatment, and is usually supported by one or more of: lid retraction of 2 mm or more, moderate or severe soft tissue involvement, exophthalmos 3 mm or more above the normal range for race and sex, and inconstant or constant diplopia. She has lid retraction well beyond 2 mm and 4 mm of exophthalmos asymmetry.

The point of the case: the original record for this patient read 'mild'. That classification was not careless reasoning. It was a consequence of never measuring lid position. Ninety seconds of bedside measurement moves her into a different treatment category and a different conversation.

On D: MRI adds activity information, not severity. Severity is a bedside determination.

Final classification: Graves' disease with inactive, moderate-to-severe Graves' orbitopathy.

steps.title: Step 8/10: The Right Operation at the Wrong Moment
steps.scenario: Inactive, moderate-to-severe Graves' orbitopathy in a 43-year-old woman who still smokes, whose TSH receptor antibody is rising, and whose thyroid function is close to but not at target on methimazole.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: (A) Start intravenous methylprednisolone on a 4.5 g cumulative twelve-week protocol and reassess
(B) Refer for orbital radiotherapy with a concurrent oral corticosteroid course
(C) Counsel smoking cessation, confirm stable euthyroidism with endocrinology, treat the ocular surface, and reassess for rehabilitative surgery once she has been stable for at least six months
(D) Book endoscopic transnasal orbital decompression at this visit

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

Options A and B are treatments for active disease. Directing anti-inflammatory therapy at an orbit with a CAS of 1 exposes her to steroid or radiation toxicity with nothing to suppress. This is the error that follows directly from conflating severity with activity: moderate-to-severe sounds like it demands action, and the activity score is what tells you which action.

Option D is the most instructive wrong answer, because it is the operation she may eventually need, chosen at the wrong point in the sequence. Rehabilitative surgery follows a fixed order: decompression, then strabismus surgery, then eyelid surgery. It requires disease that has been inactive and stable, ideally in a patient who has stopped smoking and is reliably euthyroid. Decompressing now risks a strabismus result that has to be revised, in a woman whose diplopia is currently confined to extreme upgaze.

Smoking cessation is not a footnote here. It is the single most modifiable determinant of her orbital course.

steps.title: Step 9/10: The Decision That Belongs to You
steps.scenario: Six months later she remains stable. Her endocrinologist proposes teprotumumab for the residual proptosis and asks you to see her before the first infusion.
steps.question: What is your responsibility as the otolaryngologist?

options.text: (A) Baseline audiogram, specific counseling on hearing impairment and tinnitus, and a monitoring plan with predefined stopping criteria
(B) Baseline nasal endoscopy to exclude sinonasal pathology before systemic therapy
(C) Baseline flexible laryngoscopy to document vocal fold mobility
(D) No otolaryngology assessment is needed; monitoring is the prescribing physician's responsibility

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor inhibition is associated with hearing impairment, tinnitus, and autophony. Audiologic baseline and monitoring is the one decision in thyroid eye disease that belongs to otolaryngology and to no other specialty, and defining the stopping criteria before therapy starts is more useful than discovering them afterward.

Also discuss with the referring team: hyperglycemia risk, and confirmation that she is not pregnant and is using contraception.

A note on the drug itself, worth raising rather than skipping: teprotumumab was studied in active, moderate-to-severe disease, and this patient's disease is inactive. There is subsequent evidence of proptosis reduction in chronic disease, so this is a discussion about applicability rather than a straightforward yes or no. That distinction is the same skill the last step tests.

Verify the current prescribing information before using this step in a live session, as the hearing-related labeling has been revised since approval.

steps.title: Step 10/10: What the Study Actually Showed
steps.scenario:
Actual outcome. This patient underwent total thyroidectomy approximately six months after starting antithyroid drug therapy, and was followed for roughly two years without relapse.

You selected the guideline-concordant plan. Her real management diverged from it. Before answering, consider what could justify that divergence: goiter size, methimazole intolerance, relapse risk, antibody trajectory, plans for pregnancy, and her own preference after an informed discussion.

The presentation this case came from cited a study by Meyer zu Hoerste and colleagues: 92 patients with active Graves' orbitopathy and CAS of 4 or more, comparing early thyroidectomy against continued antithyroid drug therapy, retrospectively.
steps.media: Load image: Follow-up frontal photograph, matched pose and lighting to the Step 1 image, displayed side by side at identical scale.
steps.question: Which limitation most restricts the application of that study to this patient?

options.text: (A) It was retrospective, so treatment allocation was not randomized
(B) A sample of 92 is too small to detect a modest difference between groups
(C) The enrolled population had active disease with CAS of 4 or more, while this patient's disease is inactive
(D) Orbital outcomes were assessed by clinicians who were not masked to treatment

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

The other three options are all genuine limitations of the study. That is deliberate: this item cannot be answered by spotting the one flawed choice. It requires holding this patient's phenotype in mind while reading, which is the actual skill.

A study answers a question about the population it enrolled. This patient would not have met its entry criteria. The study can be used to discuss a possible relationship between thyroidectomy and the orbital course in active disease; it cannot be used to argue that a woman with inactive, moderate-to-severe disease should have her thyroid removed.

Evidence pearl: the treatment a real patient received is an outcome, not evidence. Her two years without relapse tell you what happened to her. They do not tell you what should happen to the next patient.

Debriefing question for the group: nobody in this room recommended a thyroidectomy, and she had one. Who was wrong?
